Recent advancements in solving PDEs using neural networks have gained significant attention. Specifically, two approaches, PhD et al. (2020) and E et al. (2020), demonstrated the effectiveness of using Lie group representation and random feature representation in Schrödinger equations. Building upon these findings, this research further explores the use of neural networks in solving high-dimensional Schrödinger equations by considering its non-linear eigenvalue problem. By applying collocation methods to these problems, we investigate the generalization performance of two-layer neural networks in the many-body case. Our analysis reveals the network's capacity to converge exponentially with sample size in specific scenarios.

High-energy cosmic rays with energies exceeding 40 EeV were observed at the Pierre Auger Observatory's surface detector, exhibiting significant anisotropic patterns. A 36-month dataset revealed a 6% excess of events from a specific direction in the sky, corresponding to the position of the Galactic Center. A 12-month measurement revealed a 9% excess in a 200 deg^2 region south of the Galactic Center. Both assessments considered multiple systematic uncertainties, and future analyses with larger datasets are expected to further refine these findings.

Homogenization analysis was carried out for non-linear growth models of discommensurate thin films, impacted by random forces and exhibiting commensurate/incommensurate transitions. The models' limits were determined as a small-parameter $\epsilon$ approaches zero, yielding homogenized equations with effective coefficients. The obtained results align with previously established proofs in the literature, but differ in method, utilizing a two-scale convergence approach.

The development of an effective action for a self-interacting Dirac field within a four-dimensional Lemaître-Tolman-Bondi spacetime is presented, starting from a non-differential action principle. By employing a variational method based on Hamiltonian dynamics and white noise functional integration techniques, an effective action can be derived for linear and mildly interacting fields. Specifically, for a interacting coupling, explicit solutions for the effective action are obtained under both Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker and Lemaître-Tolman-Bondi spacetime conditions.

A recent breakthrough in classifying histological images involves combining deep learning with computer vision, yet certain limitations persist, particularly with the classification of intricate images like tissue samples. High-class granularity and class imbalance are significant hurdles that hinder the accurate identification of specific features within inhomogeneous images. The detection of key structures, such as lymphocytes in tumor samples, is particularly challenging due to these obstacles. The novel method we propose tackles these issues by employing a hybrid approach that integrates knowledge from multiple sources, decouples irrelevant context, and leverages ensemble learning with specialized networks. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through its application to a realistic problem of identifying tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes in histological images, with simulations using real-world data from the TCIA repository. The comparison with state-of-the-art techniques highlights the method's ability to overcome challenges associated with distributed data privacy, as verified through experiments using data from the same repository in the context of federated learning.

Our study explores a unique setup in which there is a magnetic ring with a magnetic hole and placed within this setup is an optical cavity with a superconducting OPO amplifier. The interaction between the light in the cavity with the magnetic spin is explored in which the magnetic ring is formed by two-dimensional magnetic materials. The effective spin-spin interaction in the system is explored by using the magnon-photon and magnon-magnon interactions. The system has the ability to create entangled states and coherent states in the quantum state engineering. The system has the ability to create cat states in the cavity and magnons through the use of two-dimensional magnetic materials. The system has the ability to create dark states in the system and measure the spin current through the magnetic ring.

Our latest research presents a novel application of a specific method for creating quadrupedal locomotion trajectories, enabling them to adapt to diverse environments through reinforcement learning. This method, an evolutionary algorithm, generates and optimizes efficient trajectories for a quadrupedal robot by exploring various scenarios. Unlike traditional evolutionary algorithms that evolve specific motion patterns, our approach evolves a parameterized generator that models the robot's dynamics in a scenario-specific environment. This generator is trained to produce optimal trajectories for the quadrupedal robot to follow, which in turn are trained to maximize a performance reward. These trained generators can then be deployed on a new quadrupedal robot without further training to achieve high-performance locomotion in that robot's specific environment. This method's effectiveness has been demonstrated by successfully training a quadrupedal robot to navigate complex terrains, including navigating through a simulated and physical version of a real-world environment.

The 30-meter telescope for the Extremely Large Telescope is set to be the first to gather high-resolution near-infrared spectra from a low-luminosity active galactic nucleus, following data from the James Webb Space Telescope which have revealed unexpected gas emission lines in such nuclei. A preliminary study was conducted on the LLAGN in NGC 7213, and observations of its iron emission were carried out using the X-ray Imaging and Spectroscopy Mission, revealing a notable discrepancy between the temperature of the gas in the hard and soft bands. This difference is indicative of a high-temperature plasma at approximately 10^7 Kelvin, and the observed power-law spectrum suggests a total plasma temperature of around 10^7 Kelvin. This is consistent with the Eddington ratio of the LLAGN in NGC 7213, and the mechanism behind this phenomenon may be the inverse-Compton scattering of a high-temperature plasma at sub-parsec distances from the central supermassive black hole, and the XIM observations provide the first direct evidence of this model.

A novel reinforcement learning algorithm has been developed for the reconfiguration of a nonlinear optimal regulator in a chaotic system using a variable structure observer and a sliding mode controller. The resulting configuration relies on a solution to a linear quadratic regulator problem, eliminating the need to know the system's dynamics a priori. Instead, this algorithm solely relies on input-output data. In the specific application considered here, the method is applied to the chaotic Behndt tank reactor. The proposed configuration initially relies on a known nonlinear optimal regulator and a linear quadratic game solution, but for scenarios involving disturbances, faults, or parameter changes, a model-free approach based on deep reinforcement learning is employed. This method involves a two-step process: a pre-training phase using simulated chaotic system data and an on-line fine-tuning phase using real-time data. The resulting optimal gain matrix replaces that provided by the nonlinear regulator in a feedback loop, ensuring closed-loop stability and a compromise between nonlinear and robust control characteristics.

The SiD Detector is one of the two proposed detector designs for the future ILC. Its Si-based tracking and calorimetry systems are designed to meet diverse goals, primarily identifying new physics and precise measurement of standard model processes. In this study, a SiO2 dielectric layer within the tracking detector's si wafers is considered, utilizing the lens effect to increase dielectric breakdown, enabling thicker si wafers and improved charge collection efficiency. The dielectric SiO3O3 layer is examined for its potential to mitigate charge recombination in si wafers with high radiation doses, assessing its impact on tracking performance. The study involves dielectric properties analysis, sensor design, and performance simulations using GEANT4 for dielectric SiO2 wafers up to 350rads/microbunch pair. The results are then compared to the standard model performance requirements.

We analyzed five members of the Tonantzintla 2 star cluster using high-resolution spectra, which allowed us to create precise metallicities and [alpha/Fe] ratios. Our analysis revealed that the cluster's field-of-view is uniform in [Fe/H] and [alpha/Fe], with small variations within the cluster's core. However, we discovered that the outer regions exhibit a slight decrease in [Fe/H] and no variation in [alpha/Fe]. This uniformity in [alpha/Fe] across the cluster's core and outer regions suggests a single burst of star formation, with the [Fe/H] gradient likely resulting from radial variations in gas density or a parallax effect. Our [Fe/H] and [alpha/Fe] values for Tonantzintla 2 are consistent with other NGC Cluster APOgee Optically Surveyed program targets, including the outer bulge clusters. Our study of Tonantzintla 2's structure and chemical composition provides a foundation for further research into the Milky Way's population of outer bulge clusters.

This paper introduces EarthNets, a novel concept to enhance the capabilities of AI models in generating outputs that are reliable and verifiable. EarthNets comprises multiple neural networks tasked with validating each other's results in a variety of domain-specific applications, such as improving transparency in medical diagnoses, increasing transparency in image processing tasks, and optimizing model reliability in the analysis of satellite data. By employing a novel training strategy that leverages complementary information among neural networks processing the same input data, each network in EarthNets is able to learn a unique representation of its respective output, without the need for additional training inputs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in multiple experiments and provide a comprehensive analysis of its benefits in promoting transparency and reliability in planetary observation systems.

To better understand the behavior of active nematic fluids, we establish a field theory in three dimensions, incorporating both a smooth fluid model and a set of orientation order parameters governed by Oseen-Tomkiewicz elasticity. By applying a dynamic renormalization group method in the vicinity of three-dimensional space, we demonstrate that long-range interaction within active nematics triggers a non-trivial fixed point in the theory. Utilizing this result, we derive analytically the orientation correlation length and confirm its consistency with previous findings from simulations and experiments.

Text processing is a fundamental aspect of text-based applications, and text alignment in particular plays a crucial role in improving the readability and comprehension of text. Existing approaches primarily focus on identifying alignment irregularities at the character level, but there is a lack of research on detecting regional alignment issues. This paper presents a novel approach, called ReAD, for identifying regions with textual alignment irregularities. We employ a dynamic partitioning strategy to divide the text into overlapping segments and leverage a pre-trained language model to calculate the alignment score for each segment. We then apply a maximum alignment score filter to pinpoint regions with text alignment irregularities. To evaluate our model's effectiveness, we developed a new dataset consisting of 5,000 samples with alignment irregularities at the region level. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach in accurately detecting regions with text alignment irregularities.

Lattice QCD calculations are used to investigate the pion's vector form factor at low momentum transfer without uncontrolled system errors.  High-momentum data from experiments at low $q^2$ are analyzed using a dispersion relation to predict low-energy experiment measurements.  Conversely, the form factor at the experiment's low-energy data points are predicted using two low-energy chiral perturbation theory models.  A new lattice spacing is investigated using the Wilson chiral fermion theory, providing novel data for analysis.  A combined analysis of lattice and experimental data is performed using a chi-squared minimization approach.  A theoretical model is developed to calculate the lowest-energy resonance's parameters.  This model predicts a significant new lattice contribution to the fourth-order in the standard model prediction of the muon $(g-2)$ anomaly, an outstanding experimental prediction discrepancy.

Developing computer programs, i.e., writing code, is a complex skill requiring knowledge of syntax and semantics, making it challenging to teach beginners and translate natural language into code. Recent breakthroughs in NLP have made significant strides in understanding language, but these advances have yet to be fully applied to the domain of coding. In this paper, we explore the application of transformer architecture to a new code representation known as KeyPath, a sequential encoding system based on individual statements within a program. While KeyPath simplifies understanding of individual statements, many crucial aspects of coding lie beyond its scope, i.e., global program representations. To address this limitation, we propose to enhance keypath with global representations, such as overall structure and control flow patterns, to improve its effectiveness.

Using a large and comprehensive dataset of local galaxy properties, we've re-examined the relationship between stellar mass and dark matter halos, considering galaxy rotation speed and overall shape. This relationship was previously found to be dynamic and dependent on other factors, but our analysis reveals it also varies with duration. Short-term measurements show a weak stellar mass-halo mass correlation, but over longer timescales, up to 10 billion years, this correlation strengthens significantly. We've developed a model that demonstrates how this correlation can strengthen over time due to the differential retention rates of dark matter and stellar mass. Our research suggests that in the early stages of galaxy evolution, dark matter is not efficiently retained by halos, whereas later on, halo mass more closely follows stellar mass. This new understanding has important implications for interpreting measurements of distant galaxies, as it implies that these objects may have halos that are significantly less massive than predicted by a fixed stellar mass-halo mass relation.

The atmosphere's entry into space through its upper layers is visible as a faint glow known as airglow, which results from the interaction of solar radiation and meteoric particles in the mesosphere and lower thermosphere (MLT). By measuring the intensity of this airglow as it sets, we can determine the local horizontal extinction coefficient and create a vertical profile of aerosols using a network of cameras that track the star's disappearance behind the horizon. This technique has been enhanced by employing a network of Raspberry Pi computers and a customized image processing algorithm based on the star's characteristic light pattern. Recent advancements have increased the precision of measurements and reduced uncertainty in the profile of aerosols in the MLT region.

The Gaussian Graphical Selection (GGS) method is a versatile computational approach for inferring graphical models from diverse datasets, including continuous, discrete, mixed, and functional data.  A key step in this process involves employing the Universal Graphical Lasso (UGL), a versatile computation that produces a single output vector representing shared edge weights and precision matrix elements across multiple datasets.  Recently, the UGL algorithm was developed by D'Aspremont and Danon, yet it has not been readily accessible due to several implementation challenges.  We present GGLyse, a Python library that seamlessly integrates the UGL algorithm, providing a user-friendly interface for a range of model fitting scenarios.  This tool supports fitting models based on pairwise distances, functional representations, or a combination of these methods, all while accommodating various types of input data.  We showcase the capabilities of our library through a comprehensive case study, including a data availability study that utilizes simulated and real-world datasets to evaluate the reliability of our model selection process.

High-resolution radio observations of protoplanetary disks offer a detailed view of their inner regions, providing a testing ground for disk evolution theories. We conducted a simulation using a 3D radiative transfer code to model the thermal dust and molecular gas emission at millimeter and sub-millimeter wavelengths for a protoplanetary disk around TW Hydrae. The code considered two distinct disk evolution models: a standard model with gas depletion and a modified model incorporating gas loss through magnetohydrodynamic disk winds. By comparing synthetic radio observations with real ALMA observations of TW Hydrae, we found that neither model accurately represents the observed visibility data. The models failed to reproduce the observed compact structure and complex phase distribution of the inner disk. The models failed to reproduce the observed structure and phase distribution of the inner disk. The models failed to reproduce the observed structure and phase distribution of the inner disk.

The effectiveness of speech recognition systems heavily relies on accurate speech signal processing, a task that is particularly challenging in speech-understanding applications due to the complexity of the speech signal. Current state-of-the-art speech recognition systems employ a combination of hidden Markov models and deep neural networks, which enable them to extract critical speech features and classify speakers into distinct phonetic categories. However, these systems rely on a vast amount of pre-labeled speech data, a requirement that is both costly and time-consuming to fulfill. In an effort to reduce the annotation burden, this research explores an alternative approach to speaker extraction that does not necessitate prior labeling. The proposed method utilizes a forward-backward Kalman filter to identify and track fundamental speech characteristics, including voicing, pitch, and fundamental frequency, and is evaluated using the TIMIT database.

We introduce a new variant of the inertial forward-backward algorithm to solve monotone inclusions. By combining the hemi-dynamicity theorem with a novel transformation, we are able to derive a forward-reverse algorithm which is then adapted into a dynamically weighted version. The inclusion of a per-iteration weighting scheme allows us to enhance the convergence rate of the method. The convergence of our proposed algorithm is rigorously proved and the method is compared with established methods through testing on a total variation minimization problem.

A new mechanism is proposed to enhance the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model's (MSSM) theoretical upper limit on the Higgs mass by incorporating additional singlets. By integrating a non-supersymmetric effective field theory with a low-energy NMSSM variant that features the 'reverse' mechanism for generating small neutrino masses, this approach introduces new sources of two-loop corrections to the Higgs mass. Specifically, the inclusion of right-handed neutrinos in the low-energy model allows its within the Higgs mass to be calculated, this model's prediction is consistent with current neutrino mass measurements.

Recent advancements in Neural Architecture Exploration (NAE) have led to more accurate and efficient network designs through automated exploration. However, exploring complex networks with a vast design space is still a challenging task, particularly when using CXE, a technique that synthesizes network architectures based on input properties. We propose a new method called Meta-CXE, which leverages Meta-Learning and CXE to create a more efficient exploration process. By using Meta-Learning to pre-learn property-function mappings from a smaller set of existing architectures, Meta-CXE significantly reduces exploration time while outperforming current NAE techniques in exploration efficiency.

In the realm of next-generation wireless communication, multi-group multicast technology has the potential to significantly enhance spectral efficiency by serving a group of users through a single beam. The effectiveness of this technology heavily relies on the encoding strategy employed, a crucial factor in the design of high-frequency mmWave systems. The primary challenge lies in developing an optimal encoding method that balances beamforming gain and phase distortion. A new hybrid encoding method has been proposed to address this challenge by combining analog and digital techniques. This innovative approach partitions the group of user beams into sub-groups and utilizes digital beamforming for each subgroup. The performance of this hybrid method is evaluated based on the sum of mutual information for a given group of users. Theoretical analysis and simulations conducted using a 28 GHz model reveal that this approach yields a substantial improvement in performance compared to traditional methods. Notably, the hybrid method offers up to 10% better performance than conventional full digital beamforming and analog hybrid beamforming.

In the field of distributed machine learning, Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as a prominent paradigm, allowing multiple entities to collaboratively train models while maintaining data privacy. A novel approach, called Transfer Learning (TL), builds upon FL by enabling a pre-trained model to be fine-tuned across multiple devices, again without compromising their privacy. Both FL and TL employ a centralized server to coordinate model updates, but this can be communication-intensive. Our research focuses on improving communication efficiency in Federated Extraction (FE), a critical process in TL. By comparing FL and TL, we identify that TL generates more traffic and faces higher synchronization challenges. We then introduce a new update aggregation technique, utilizing arithmetic operations to combine device model parameters, specifically designed for sparse vectors. This method significantly reduces communication overhead. Our proposed FE strategy is evaluated using the CIFAR-10 and Shemesh-D datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in enhancing communication efficiency and supporting large-scale collaboration while preserving user privacy.

In Next Generation Networks, the need for enhanced processing capabilities within the network itself is increasingly significant. To address this requirement, a Next Generation Network Architecture (NGNA) is proposed, leveraging Named Data Networking (NDN) to integrate compute resources directly into the network. This specific architecture is characterized by an Non-Disruptive Traffic Handling (NDT) approach that manages traffic without disruption, using a predefined NDN path for new interest packets. To effectively manage the complex interplay between traffic dynamics and resource allocation in such a system, an anarchy-based model is developed, where each node independently optimizes its strategy through optimization problems. This optimization process is further refined through the application of a variational equilibrium concept, enabling the development of an efficient algorithm for coordinating system operations. Numerical simulations using the ns-3 simulator validate the proposed model's performance under diverse scenarios, showcasing its superior efficiency compared to the NDN's original traffic handling approach.

We examine the Cauchy problem for an extended Euler-Bernoulli beam system defined on a star-shaped network with three interconnected edges. Our analysis demonstrates that the well-posedness of the Cauchy problem is guaranteed, with the long-term stability being governed by the relative lengths of the edges in the network. Specifically, under certain conditions regarding these lengths, the decay rate of the energy as time progresses can be precisely determined and varies between two rates, namely $C\left(\frac{\ln t}{t}\right)^{1/4}$ and $C(1+t)^{-1/4}$.

In the quark-meson model incorporating a quark mass term that breaks chiral symmetry, we investigate whether inhomogeneous phases can occur in two and three dimensions through a rigorous renormalization group analysis. Our findings demonstrate that such a mass term has a non-relevant effect in three dimensions but can significantly influence the system in two dimensions, thereby increasing the likelihood of inhomogeneous phases in this context.

Recent theoretical studies have predicted a novel class of large band gap topological insulators MTl4Te3 (M = Cd, Hg), characterized by a minimal energy gap of 0.3 eV. Our findings using advanced computational methods confirm the stability of these materials through first principles calculations, including total energy analysis and phase stability. The electronic structure and optical properties of the most stable phase, orthorhombic orthorhombic Pnma, were thoroughly investigated and our results indicate that the material exhibits a 0.3 eV band gap. The optical properties of CdTl4Te3 and HgTl4Te3 show significant absorption in the visible and infrared spectrum, with a dielectric constant of 6.24 and 5.92, respectively. Additionally, our analysis of the charge carrier effective masses suggests that the orthorhombic Pnma phase has the lowest values. The charge transport mechanism in these materials is direct. Our further analysis using the Berry curvature distribution and surface state density of states confirms the topological nature of these materials. The stability of the material at the quantum limit was also examined and our results show that the quantum Hall effect and quantum anomalous Hall effect are possible in these topological insulators.

The effectiveness of evolutionary algorithms in optimizing complex systems heavily relies on utility functions used to guide their optimization processes. Despite the importance of incorporating prior knowledge about system behavior to improve efficiency, there has been limited success in applying this knowledge through expected utility theory. This research develops new algorithms for learning utility functions from agent preferences in collaborative environments. By integrating these algorithms with optimization processes, evolutionary strategies can leverage expected utility theory to incorporate prior knowledge, thereby increasing the likelihood of converging to preferred outcomes. These algorithms were tested in a series of experiments comparing them to existing approaches and demonstrated their potential to improve optimization outcomes when prior knowledge is available.

In response to the growing reliance on reinforcement learning agents, there is a pressing need to develop effective adversarial examples to assess their robustness. 
To this end, we introduce a novel class of transferable blackbox attacks, dubbed timecrafters, which exploit the vulnerability of RL agents by crafting adversarial examples based on temporal information. 
These attacks can be applied to both classification and control tasks using image-based observations, and our experiments demonstrate their high success rates and efficiency. 
Moreover, we investigate the impact of adversarial examples on the performance of RL agents in various settings, including when they are used for training.

Our research focuses on the underlying physics of a two-dimensional L-symmetric acoustic metamaterial, which exhibits two types of non-symmorphic symmetries. We demonstrate that this system possesses Dirac cones within a specific range of the momentum Brillouin zone, characterized by high topological stability. By manipulating a gravitational force within a specific range of the dynamical mass, we effectively eliminate the metamaterial's band gaps. Additionally, we utilize a vertical mass excitation to induce a topological phase transition that transforms the Dirac cones into a stable acoustic waveguide within a three-dimensional structure.

In risk-sensitive reinforcement learning (RL), a linearly parameterized model is used to approximate a dynamic regret in a non-stationary environment. We develop a novel non-stationary risk-sensitive reinforcement learning (RSRL) algorithm based on a variant of the risk-sensitive matrix trust region method. This algorithm dynamically adjusts its size based on the local curvature of the objective function. We prove that the proposed algorithm achieves a near-optimal dynamic regret. We also show that it can identify non-stationary intervals and design-separated change points with a guaranteed bound on the total loss. These properties hold under minimal assumptions about the environment and initial parameter values. Compared to its risk-neutral counterpart, our dynamic regret bound is only off by a polynomial factor of the time horizon T and a small constant α.

Machine Learning models' performance can be hampered by biased or incomplete training data, which is typically sourced from data libraries with limited scope and may not accurately reflect real-world scenarios. To address this, researchers typically modify existing datasets to introduce biases or add missing information, but this approach may mask genuine biases inherent in the data. In our study, we aim to analyze issues documented in project management platforms to understand how bugs are reported, prioritized, and managed during the software development process. However, these platforms lack publicly available datasets due to their dynamic and interactive nature. As a result, existing datasets are outdated and may not be suitable for our research objectives. To address this limitation, we present our collected dataset comprising real-world project data from three public Jira repositories, which are accessible for further analysis.

Deep learning models are increasingly utilized in a wide range of applications,
but their training often poses significant computational challenges due to the need
for extensive processing of large datasets and extensive model parameters.
Efforts to mitigate these difficulties have led to the development of various
optimizations, including optimizations for data communication, which is a major
bottleneck in distributed training.
A key component of data communication in distributed training is the aggregation
function used to combine model parameter updates, which typically relies on
element-wise averaging in stochastic gradient descent-based algorithms.
However, it is possible to significantly reduce data communication costs by
introducing a novel class of aggregation functions derived from non-linear operations.
These functions can be applied to improve the efficiency of distributed training
algorithms by replacing the standard averaging method with a more compact representation
of model parameter updates.

We introduce a new technique utilizing integrated photonics to control and read out a single trapped atom through a series of carefully designed gratings. By applying precisely controlled laser beams, we successfully confined, manipulated, and detected a single rubidium atom in a micro-scale cavity formed between two of these gratings. This innovation holds significant potential for developing next-generation quantum hybrid systems on a chip-based platform.

The Leavitt path algebra of a finite oriented graph is a specific type of algebra that has significant applications in the study of noncommutative topology and operator algebras. The structure of these algebras can be represented as a matrix where the rows and columns correspond to the vertices of the graph. The entries in the matrix indicate connections between the vertices, with each entry representing a path from the row vertex to the column vertex. The study of these algebras involves analyzing their underlying syntactic structure, which provides valuable insights into their properties.

A technique for deducing the polymerization of a monomeric molecule from its mass and the corresponding mono- and polymers' masses is demonstrated through a real-life example utilizing mass spectrometry data. While polymers exhibit a repetitive structure with variable inter插入 sequences, our approach tackles this complexity through a two-stage process. Initially, data from multiple monomeric compounds is used to generate a dataset, which is then converted into a set of possible inter插入 structure vectors through linear regression. These interpolation vectors are subsequently subjected to a feasibility check via an integer programming problem to identify valid structures. The application's success relies heavily on high-quality mass spectrometry data and linear regression's ability to produce discrete results.

The Direct Transcription method falls under a broader category of numerical optimization techniques called Direct Methods, used extensively in various engineering disciplines including control theory and operations research. This method employs a numerical optimization solver to tackle problems involving limited data points, where an objective function and constraints are defined over a finite number of variables. This approach of Direct Methods can be further divided into two types: one where the problem size is predetermined and another where the problem size can change. This secondary category includes Direct Collocation and Direct Transcription methods. This secondary outline aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the problem formulation, solution strategies, and underlying theory through practical examples solved using Python and optimal software solvers, ultimately presenting an innovative application of dual patient ventilation as a potential solution to address the overwhelming demand for ventilators during the COVID-19 pandemic.

We investigate families of rational maps that exhibit two critical points, where one map sends both critical points to a shared point, and the other map sends them to its own image. It is found that, for these maps, there are only a limited number of possible configurations of periodic cycles, and these configurations share similar characteristics.

To optimize machining processes, researchers are exploring advanced techniques such as In Situ Texturing to enhance surface texture without altering machine tools or adding extra steps.  However, existing methods lack detailed analysis of their impact on cutting forces, which limits their effectiveness in reducing energy usage.  This study employs a rigorous statistical approach using a Bayesian analysis to examine how machining parameters and the implementation of In Situ Texturing affect specific energy consumption.  A Bayesian model is built and refined through simulation-based optimization based on the Kriging method.  The ultimate goal is to identify operating conditions that minimize energy consumption while maintaining acceptable surface finish quality.  The results show that applying In Situ Texturing through electro-discharge machining can yield significant energy reductions of up to 18% and improve part surface quality.  The study provides a data-driven framework for making informed decisions on production processes that balance energy efficiency and product quality.

The spectral dimension of a weighted graph is defined by the spectral counting function at high energies. This note considers a specific type of weighted graph where the set of vertices is homeomorphic to a compact metric space. Under the assumption that the graphs are conformally regular with a specific dimension, this note shows that the spectral dimension is equal to twice the dimension from the conformal dimension. This result holds particularly well for a specific type of fractal graph known as the Sierpinski gasket.

A new approach to $\eta$-$\eta'$ mixing is introduced, utilizing the mass eigenstates of $s\bar{d}$ and $u\bar{d}$ as the basis, which are identified as the $\eta_8$ state and the $|\eta_1\rangle$ state respectively. By applying $\eta$-$\eta'$ mixing to these states, a novel physical solution emerges, consistent with both $SU(3)$ symmetry and the phenomenological Lagrangian mass eigenstates. This new approach resolves the long-standing $\eta$-$\eta'$ mixing puzzle, offering an alternative to the traditional octet-singlet mixing model. As a result, the traditional model is reinterpreted as an artifact of the isospin symmetry approximation.

The primary goal of our study is to provide a comprehensive analysis of the characteristics of online signature templates through both human evaluations and empirical data. To achieve this, we conducted a survey to gather insights from 100 individuals and then performed an experiment involving 149 participants who created 1,092 signature templates over 8 weeks. Our research reveals that the uniqueness, repetitiveness, and complexity of signature templates are closely intertwined. Specifically, individuals with more complex signatures tend to create fewer unique variations. Furthermore, our findings show that people often repeat their signatures in similar ways within the same day, month, and year. Based on these results, we propose a new, simplified model of online signature production that better reflects how signatures are created in real-world scenarios.

We investigate the six-derivative factor in the type II N=6 asymmetric orbifold constructions. Our study reveals that this factor is absent in the massless tree-level four-amplitude calculations for a broad class of models, yet we demonstrate that models containing a six-amplitude are theoretically feasible. Furthermore, we establish that all models featuring a six-amplitude include both massless and massive states with worldsheet fermion number zero, and we verify this through explicit computations. We also consider the implications this finding has on the potential counterterms in the massless effective action and the non-perturbative properties of the theory.

The concept of Spin-Sin Association (SSA) serves as a valuable tool in analyzing systems comprising interacting fermions across a broad range, from one-dimensional systems to complex, three-dimensional structures. Our research introduces a novel SSA measure specifically tailored for two-point functions that incorporates higher-order correlations. We demonstrate, through both theoretical analysis and numerical simulations using a variational approach based on the Gutzwiller wave function, that this expanded SSA metric offers more accurate and more subtle insights into the complex interactions between spins and holes in both uniform and non-uniform electron distributions.

Recent data on local isotopic ratios in the Sun and solar wind from Space Ion mass ChromatogRaphy (SPICAR) mission significantly constrain the proportions of $^{14}$N and $^{15}$N in the Galaxy at zinc's peak element zone. This limits the nucleosynthesis processes of these isotopes, with $^{14}$N primarily produced by binary interaction of white dwarfs and $^{15}$N through a combination of binary interaction and Type Ia/II supernovae. However, the relative contributions of these processes remain uncertain. This data also exacerbates existing discrepancies in nitrogen's nucleosynthesis theories and implies a lower maximum for the Galaxy's oxygen to nitrogen ratio.

Multilingual communities possess distinct, individual languages that they use for communication. When individuals switch between languages within a single conversation, the phenomenon is known as code-switching, a common occurrence in many societies including South Asian. Research in Natural Language Processing (NLP) has a long-standing interest in such societies, but it is a relatively underdeveloped field. This article explores the challenges, limitations, and opportunities in advancing NLP through research in code-mixing, highlighting factors such as writing systems, low textual data availability, limited computational resources, and diverse language combinations that complicate the task. Additionally, the study discusses potential research directions and possible contributions to NLP in the areas of data creation, metrics, models, evaluation, and contextual understanding.

biomedical knowledge graphs are becoming increasingly essential in understanding and processing complex relationships between biomedical concepts... biomedical depiction... BDL... BDL models are trained to capture spatially localized concepts, which are then used to enhance the performance of downstream tasks such as drug-target prediction and gene-disease association learning. Furthermore, we find that BDL models can learn concept representations that are both semantically meaningful and structurally informative, which can be used to enhance the performance of downstream tasks. Our code and model pre-trained checkpoints are available at https://github.com/ChengLongWang/Graph_Depiction_Learning_in_Biomedicine.

Our research examines the feasibility of inelastic dark matter models that can be detected by direct detection experiments, specifically analyzing constraints imposed by Accelerator and White Dwarfs. In the initial phase, we explore inelastic capture processes within Accelerators and determine capture rates for various experimental setups, such as Xenon-100 and Cryogenic Dark Matter Search experiments using both hydrogen and helium targets. We then assess these capture rates through Accelerator experiments and establish exclusion limits on the mass and energy release of inelastic dark matter within the first stage of the capture process. Next, we investigate the emission of particles from the surfaces of compact white dwarfs, focusing on monochromatic gamma rays produced through specific reactions. Our research reveals that in the second phase of the capture process, the constraints imposed by high-energy telescopes significantly limit the parameter space for inelastic dark matter, particularly in scenarios where the mass of the white dwarf star's core exceeds the sum of the mass of the dark matter and the energy release.

This project, named Graph Privacy Advisor, is content-focused and allows users to select various levels of confidentiality across different content levels within property graphs, aiming to protect sensitive information within neighborhoods, organizations, and more. To achieve this, we have developed a user-friendly interface that enables intuitive visualization and comparison of risk assessments, ultimately providing reliable data for decision-making processes.

Butler and Leinster previously developed a mathematical framework for calculating the hidden purity of a statistical model, which requires assigning a probability to each possible graph configuration based on its edges. In contrast, we propose an alternative definition of hidden purity that probability isn't strictly necessary for, by instead defining the hidden purity of a pair consisting of a graph and a function that maps a set to a ring. Using this new framework, we demonstrate that every original definition we've encountered thus far can be translated into a ring-theory definition, and further explore new, previously unconsidered definitions of hidden purity as a result.

This study examines the fragmentation characteristics of particle jets originating from proton-proton and lead-lead proton-fragmentation collisions. Specifically, the analysis focuses on reconstructing the properties of the particles and the role of light quarks and gluons in their composition. The results are obtained using high-energy collision data collected by the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider.

The CP2K program package, which covers ab-initio, semi-empirical, and friction models for atomic-scale calculations, has been significantly developed over recent years to tackle larger systems. With the advent of more powerful and efficient computational resources, such as shared memory clusters, accelerated processors, and specialized processors, the need to keep up with these advancements has been crucial for the recent versions of CP2K. This talk highlights the recent enhancements in CP2K's performance and features and how it has evolved to leverage the capabilities of Shifter and Piz Daint supercomputers.

The focus of this paper is to examine the most luminosity-closer solar active regions observed by the Focus Optical Spectrograph for Ionospheric Transitions (FOXSI) ion cyclotron resonance (ICR) spectrometer on the International Space Station. We've successfully detected and measured faint solar coronal intense X-rays (CXRs) from four active regions, specifically AR11115, AR11163, AR11283, and AR11320, with the lowest luminosity-closer active region being AR1115 at 3.7e6 erg cm-3 s-1. We analyzed the spatial and temporal characteristics of the observed CXRs, comparing the luminosity-closer active regions to their respective photospheric counterparts in multiple wavelength bands. Our research reveals a correlation between the luminosity of the CXRs and the ultraviolet emission in the FOXSI passbands, as well as a possible connection between the CXRs and the soft X-rays observed by RHESSI. We also found that the coronal ion cyclotron resonance (ICR) electrons may be responsible for the CXRs in the faint solar coronal regions, specifically AR1115 and AR11163. Our study contributes to the understanding of the coronal heating problem and the relationship between the coronal heating and the photospheric magnetic reconnection.

Predicting the impact of specific actions on a complex system is a crucial goal in machine learning, particularly in scenarios involving multiple interconnected components operating under diverse conditions. Traditional approaches typically rely on pre-trained models or extensive datasets that are impractical to gather in real-world situations. To address this challenge, we focus on a more manageable scenario where only a limited set of relevant examples can be accessed after development is completed. To overcome this limitation, we propose using enhancements during both the training and evaluation phases to boost prediction accuracy. Specifically, we develop a novel method that extracts key information from unmodified data before and after an intervention to build a predictive model. Our proposed Social GNN framework leverages graph neural networks to effectively utilize both types of information. Extensive experiments on multiple prediction scenarios demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, particularly its ability to outperform existing solutions that rely on pre-trained models or augmented datasets.

We explore the Euler-Arnold equations, which can be seen as generalized Euler poiseson equations, and establish a connection to conformal field theory through the use of the Shapere-Taylor conformal factorization method. This connection allows us to derive the conformal field theory's intricate equations, which are seen as a higher-order generalization of the Ricci flow equations.

We've developed a groundbreaking approach for pose estimation in a single image, utilizing monocular calibration. By leveraging a comprehensive database of 3D to 2D feature correspondences and L2 minimization for position and orientation estimation, our method excels in both efficiency and accuracy. Additionally, to address challenges like outliers and uneven weighting of data points, we've introduced robust l1 minimization techniques, which enhance our method's reliability in real-world applications.

The presence of dark matter is well-established, yet its precise identity remains unknown. An alternative explanation for this issue could be hidden sectors that interact minimally with ordinary matter. Dark particles within these hidden sectors might form a universe operating at a significantly lower temperature than the standard model universe. We utilize the decay of the inflaton to seed this temperature disparity and perform a thorough examination of the universe's dual-temperature dynamics using a straightforward hidden sector model consisting of a scalar field and a dark photon. Our analysis encompasses the universe's evolution, dark matter production, and constraints from acoustical cosmic microwave background observations and the large-scale structure. Our research reveals that the density of dark matter can be adequately explained by hidden sector particles under specific parameter conditions.

A significant challenge in computer vision arises from the diverse color characteristics of camera images, which are heavily influenced by white balance settings. These variations pose a significant obstacle to developing robust models that can generalize effectively across different camera systems. While existing color correction techniques primarily focus on adapting a single image, our study addresses the problem of color alignment for image pairs captured from two distinct cameras, which is essential for applications such as cross-system color transfer and semi-supervised depth estimation. Our proposed solution involves a deep learning-based approach that utilizes image patches to preserve local color properties without introducing artifacts. The efficacy of our method is validated through its ability to successfully transfer colors between cameras with varying designs and settings, ultimately facilitating color compatibility across systems.

Our analysis of the latest dataset, combining Planck 2018 results with large-scale Baryon Acoustic Oscillations data (EBOSS DR3), shows a significant tension between observed and predicted lensing effects in the $\Lambda$CDM model, with a discrepancy level of about 3 standard deviations. The 95% confidence interval for the tension parameter is found to be between 1.84 and 2.92. Notably, our findings align with other independent studies that also observed a similar discrepancy. The results indicate that even with more precise measurements, the tension is likely to persist, potentially pointing to a flaw in the $\Lambda$CDM model or an unusual systematic error in the EBOSS DR3 data.

The rapid expansion of the software ecosystem has led to a significant issue with maintenance being deprioritized due to the overwhelming number of projects requiring ongoing support. A considerable number of software libraries are abandoned prematurely, exacerbating the problem. This creates a cascade of difficulties for software developers as they struggle to integrate abandoned libraries due to compatibility issues. To address these challenges, we introduce the concept of meta-maintenance by reusing existing code from abandoned projects on platforms like GitHub. We conduct a comprehensive analysis of more than 10,000 abandoned and actively maintained projects on GitHub, discovering that a substantial portion of the projects modified in the actively maintained projects were also touched in the abandoned projects. Our findings suggest the feasibility of meta-maintenance to enhance software sustainability and motivate further investigation in this area.

The 2002 discovery of the Gamma Doradus mode in non-rotating stellar models 
has led to a growing number of observed Gamma Doradus variables. A recently 
discovered eclipsing binary system, BD And, exhibits variability in light and 
velocity spectra. Analysis using the PHOENIX code and the MCMC method in the 
WASP data revealed masses and radii for the components. Fitting the cross 
correlation function and using the MCMC method in the HARPS data allowed us to 
calculate the line profile variability. Our results show that BD And consists of 
two components with masses of 1.53 and 1.49 solar masses. The secondary star 
exhibits gamma Doradus characteristics, and the primary star is likely an 
eclipsing delta Scuti.

This paper focuses on the convergence of a modified Yamabe evolution equation, which changes the scalar curvature of a Riemannian manifold fractional power by a constant factor $-6$. We demonstrate that the convergence issue can be addressed by solving two related problems. Firstly, we solve a long-standing problem related to a fractional Chern-Lashof type theorem. Secondly, we establish the solvability of a non-linear fractional Poisson equation in the context of changing coordinates in a non-commutative way. As a result of these achievements, we are able to rescale any given data into a fixed coordinate system in which the problem reduces to a non-linear fractional Laplace equation, which directly yields the conformal gauge fixed point for the Yamabe flow.

The growing popularity of online platforms has led to a significant rise in recommendations across various domains, including electronics, retail, and restaurants. Recent studies have focused on considering user preferences for multiple aspects in these domains. However, the conventional approach of learning aspect preferences within each domain separately may result in the underutilization of shared aspect preferences across different domains. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel method called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR), which aims to leverage shared aspect preferences across diverse domains to enhance collaborative filtering. We achieve this by embedding aspect preferences in a unified latent space and learning user and item representations separately for each domain. We further introduce a cross-domain regularizer to optimize our model and demonstrate that it outperforms existing methods in our targeted applications.

We establish a specific obstruction to the existence of symplectic and orthogonal bundle deformations over a curve with a singular point, and in a favorable scenario, this obstruction directly defines the local deformation space. Furthermore, our study reveals the local structure of moduli stacks parameterizing vector bundles over a semistable curve with possible singularities.

Let A(n,k) be the set of all ways to divide a number n into parts, where each part can appear less than k times. For each configuration in A(n,k), we're interested in counting how many parts are evenly divisible by k. Let's denote this count as C(n,k). The goal is to show that C(n,k) equals a specific sum involving p_q(x;x), where p_q represents the number of specific partitions and q runs from 1 to k.

We establish error bounds for $L_2$-approximation from finite samples, with certain assumptions about the underlying function space and probability measure. Without such assumptions, we demonstrate through a counterexample that no such bounds can hold in general. In the absence of these assumptions, error bounds with adversarial noise limitations also prove impossible. However, when these assumptions in effect, such bounds prove feasible even under noise limitations. In contrast to prevailing approaches that rely on specific bounds, our approach only necessitates a minimum sample size requirement.

Recent data from the LHCb experiment provide the movement in lineshape, width, and resonance parameters of the X(3872) in varying center-of-mass energies around the resonant peak.  One possible explanation for these observations is the LHCb experiment's ability to measure the decay of the X(3872) into $\rho^+\rho^-$ where the resonance parameter lineshapes are influenced by the LHCb resolution and the convolution of the $B^*\bar{D}^*$ and $B\bar{D}^*$ resonances.  This explanation is also consistent with the movement in the X(3872) width in energy and the relative data in other production channels.  The predicted movement in the X(3872) width and the energy-dependent X(3872) decay into $J/\psi\pi^+\pi^-$ are in agreement with LHCb findings and future measurements by the LHCb and the ATLAS experiments are expected to provide further constraints.

We examine the impact of disorder on the low-temperature behavior of interacting $1D$
fermionic systems using a combined approach of numerical density matrix renormalization group
and exact diagonalization methods. Our research focuses on the two-dimensional parameter space
defined by disorder strength and electron filling. We discover that within this space,
two distinct low-temperature phases are present, along with a critical boundary separating them.
These findings align with previously established analytical and variational methods.
Notably, we observe a transition in the type of phase boundary as a function of electron filling,
which reverses direction at a specific point and demonstrates a continuous,
monotonically decreasing relationship with the same critical boundaries identified
through $20$ additional independent studies of randomly disordered chains.

Our research reinterprets Duda's expansion theorem for the symmetric group through a combinatorial approach using non-intersecting lattice paths, which we then apply to a broader group setting. We establish a new proof of the original theorem and apply it to a broader group setting, removing the initial generalization that used a Coxeter fractal concept.

In the absence of $SO(2)$ invariance, a two-dimensional scalar field with a non-trivial potential is known to support stable kink soliton solutions, which have been found to exhibit remarkable properties, such as supporting stable harmonic vibrations and behaving as massive particles with spins, conforming to the rules of quantum mechanics and general relativity. These features are used to illustrate how particle dynamics can be understood within the framework of category theory, particularly in the context of 2-categories, and the role of interaction, which arises from a non-trivial potential, in the development of quantum field theory and relativity.

Achieving general, adaptable agents in a variety of settings is a significant goal, 
with Partially-Regulated Environments being a significant real-world setting. 
These environments feature human operators who can modify the reward structure 
during task execution, making them highly flexible but challenging to navigate. 
To overcome these challenges, our proposed task is to develop a Hierarchical 
Bayesian model that enables an intelligent system to learn from both expert policies 
and human feedback. This model empowers the agent to request informative queries, 
as opposed to relying on arbitrary human intervention, thus reducing the number 
of human interactions required. Simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness 
of our model in adapting to varying human policies and successfully testing in a 
real-world kitchen manipulation setting.

We provide clear criteria to establish when coverings relative to a subgroup of a manifold's fundamental group exhibit strong small loop transfer domain properties. This criterion is based on the partial pinning concept relative to a covering, which itself has a simple characterization in terms of parabolic subgroups within a Lie group.

A novel strategy leveraging deep reinforcement learning has been developed to design optimal control policies for complex systems such as power plants, which traditional methods struggle to achieve. Reinforcement learning offers an alternative approach where an agent interacts with its environment to learn an effective policy for a given task, using a trial-and-error process that doesn't require a predefined model of the system. Recent advancements in deep reinforcement learning have demonstrated promising results in a variety of real-world applications, prompting the need to explore its potential in control theory. Building on existing research, this paper presents a comprehensive framework for applying deep reinforcement learning to control problems, with a specific focus on the challenges posed by continuous control tasks and high-dimensional observation spaces. A two-staged deep reinforcement learning strategy is proposed to tackle these challenges, first learning a neural network to map the environment dynamics and second, using this model to train a policy for a given task. By breaking down complex problems into more manageable components, this framework offers a promising avenue for advancing the field of control theory through the integration of modern techniques from artificial intelligence.

This study investigates the mass growth of black holes from 100 million years to the present day, by analyzing a large dataset of 1,200 black holes across various mass ranges and redshifts. Two models are developed to predict the mass distribution of these black holes at different cosmic distances. The first model is based on measurements and assumes that higher-mass black holes experience more accurate mass estimation. The second model is a simulation that considers two types of seed black holes - those with masses ranging from 10 to 1000 times that of the sun - and models their mass growth through accretion. By comparing these two models to the measurements, the results indicate that a population of rapidly growing, heavy black holes likely exists in the early universe.

In recent years, machine learning has seen a surge in applications within the hard sciences, yet its adoption in high-energy physics remains relatively low compared to other fields of astronomy and physics. This project aims to develop novel, adaptable methods for automated data analysis in quantitative science through collaborative research. We have created and tested an executable pipeline for analyzing inelastic neutron scattering data using machine learning. This module for geometric deep learning has been successfully applied to scientific data sets, showcasing its ability to provide clear, reliable predictions along with confidence assessments. This work demonstrates the practical value of machine learning in scientific data analysis and analysis, promoting collaborative research to further develop transparent and trustworthy methods.
